content.title: How to calculate ABN?

replying_to: Replying to How to calculate ABN?

content.comment:
Thank you for your comment! Both ABN and PBN need no retraining after filter pruning. The details are as follows.

1) Retraining. Retraining is to update both the network parameters and the BN statistics by several forward and backward propagations. Using the retraining method is able to accurately evaluate the potential of the pruned model, which, however, is time-consuming. Please refer to Figure 3 (right) for detail.


2) PBN (Post-Training BN). PBN is to directly inference the pruned networks using the original/vallina BN without retraining. In the original BN, the statistics are the moving average means and variances of unpruned networks. Since there is a domain gap between the pruned and unpruned model, using the statistics of the unpruned model to evaluate the potential of the pruned model is inappropriate. See Figure 3 (left).


3) ABN (Adaptive BN). Our ABN is to recalculate BN statistics for the pruned models, but without retraining. We hypothesize that the learned knowledge is stored in the network parameters of each layer, whereas the domain shift between the pruned and unpruned model is represented by the statistics of BN layers. Therefore, we freeze all the network parameters while resetting the moving average statistics. Then, we update the moving statistics by a few iterations of forward-propagation, but without backward propagation. ABN is fast and accurate (Figure 3, middle).

Moreover, compared with the retraining method, ABN is more effortless. Because in the retraining method, a human expert is needed to select hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, weight decay).

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper addresses to prune networks by evaluating candidate pruned networks using the adaptive batch normalization (ABN). While existing methods utilizes pretrained BN parameters for evaluating pruned candidates, ABN utilizes updated BN parameters by simply forwarding a subset of training data to update the BN statistics given some pruned structure. The authors observed that the evaluation metric based on ABN is more correlated with the fine-tuned accuracy compared to that of PBN. Finally, the authors present experiments for MobileNet and ResNet.

Overall, I doubt the methodological contribution of ABN. I think that the main idea is quite similar to that of Liu et al., 2019b (the right figure of Figure 3). The proposed algorithm `fine-tunes’ only BN parameters while the algorithm in Liu et al., 2019b fine-tunes the whole parameters. Pruning entire one epoch as done in Liu et al., 2019b might be expensive, however, I believe that the training iteration could be adjusted given any computational budget. This is the main reason why my decision toward rejection.

Other comments are listed below:
-I am not clear about introducing a new correlation measure (5). Explicitly noting why the correlation based on accuracies as done in Figure 3 is not enough for the evaluation would be helpful.

-For justifying (5), the authors mentioned that searching the top-1 model is NP-hard but the top-k model is not. I could not fully understand this statement due to the following reason: If the top-1 model refers the model generating the best test accuracy given pruned architecture, searching it is NP-hard but searching one of the top k best models would be also NP-hard. If the top-1 model refers to the top-1 accuracy (or class) of the fine-tuned model (i.e., Y[1]), then it would be easily computed (i.e., not NP-hard). More explanation on NP-hardness would be helpful.

-In Section 3, there is a repeated argument `Figure 3 and Figure 3 respectively’.

- In the second paragraph of Section 4.2, Figure 4.2 is referred but there is no Figure 4.2

display_title: Reply to reviewer #1 from the authors

content.title: Reply to reviewer #1 from the authors
content.comment:
Question 1: difference with Liu et. al., 2019b. It might be expensive, but computational budget should be fine.
Answer: as mentioned in the “Related work” section, the main concern for us about (Liu et. al., 2019b) is the complex design of AutoML agent and it might require expert insights for the algorithm to perform the most. For example, there is a noise in their method that remains 0.5 in the first 100 exploration epochs and then 300 epochs of exponentially decaying. This type of tricks sets up a higher barrier to use the method. Moreover, they train a reinforcement learning agent to find the layer-wise redundancy. Training-involved pruning methods need very high computation cost compared to only a few iterations of interence required in our FNNP method. Detailed comparisons can be found in the Table 2 in our revised manuscript and the description about it. Fine-tuning a single pruned candidate might be totally fine considering modern computers' hardware resources, but doing to all the candidates in the searching space, or in multiple pruning tasks can be very time-consuming and hence impractical. 

Question 2: Not clear about equation (5) the correlation metric
Answer: thank you for point this out. We have added more description about the intuition and meaning of the items in Section 3.2. As a high-level summary, the intuition of Equation 5 is to highlight the matched high accuracy samples in both variables X and Y while ignoring the negative correlation as it is not expected trends in any evaluation process of pruning tasks. You may find more newly-added details in Section 3.2.

Question 3: why correlation based on accuracies as done in Fig 3 is not enough for evaluation
Answer: thank you for this question, which is also pointed out by other readers. We newly added Section 3.1 "Motivation" for a description with richer details. As a summary here, the global BN statistics are not adapted to the pruned network structures. So they mess up the inference accuracy during evaluation for the pruned networks. It also results in the low-range evaluation accuracy mentioend in the previous question. Adaptive BN re-calculates the BN statistocal values based on the pruned network connections, so it fixes this problem and brings the evaluation accuracy back to a normal range. Fine-tuning also does the same thing, but with a much higher computational cost (Table 2 in the revised manuscript).

Question 4: NP-hardness
Answer: thank you for your careful reading. The authors agree that top-1 and top-k have the same NP-hardness nature. This point does not contribute to any of our claims and we do not intend to imply any advantages of using top-5 ranking in correlation calculation. Therefore, we removed this from our new revised manuscript.
 
Question 5: typos and wrong references.
Answer: we have largely revised our manuscript. Apart from fixing all the typos and faults, we also rephrased “Introduction” section, re-structured “Methodology” and “Experiments” sections to show a clearer presentation about our ideas. We sincerely invite you in reading again our newly uploaded version if it does not bothers you too much. Thank you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This manuscript proposed a fast network pruning framework with an ABN-based evaluation module. The ABN module is capable of obtain the adapted mean and variance with retraining on a small sample of data. From the experiments, it is observed that the ABN module is able to catch strong correlation on test accuracy between the evaluated model and the fine-tuned model.
Following are reviewer’s comments:
1. The result is promising. The proposed evaluation method is fast and simple, achieving comparable performance on both efficiency and accuracy.
2. What does the adapted mean and variance mean? I assume it is the domain gap (shift) between the vanilla network and the pruned network, and that is the main motivation of this work. But this point is not clarified in the manuscript.
3. It is Figure 5 (left) rather than ‘Figure 4.2’ shows the correlation between iterations and accuracies.
4. This manuscript is very poor written:
On page 4: duplicate ‘Figure 3’; duplicate ‘block’; ‘helps’ should be singular.
On page 5: duplicate ‘present’; ‘the smallest filters’ should be singular.
On page 6: ‘metirc’. ‘there’ but ‘their’, ‘beteween’, ‘each constraints’ and more.

content.title: Official Blind Review #5
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
This paper studies the Neural Network Pruning problem. It proposes an FNNP method, which incorporates an Adaptive Batch Normalization (ABN) based evaluation module to connect the accuracy of pruning candidates and their final converged accuracy. The experiments show that the ABN-based sub-net evaluation module facilitates fast and accurate neural network pruning.
 
My major concern of this paper is that it fails to state the motivation to adopt adaptive BN clearly. Based on the existing statements, ABN would be fast since it recalculates the statistics for BN based on a small part of training data. And It may be accurate since this evaluation module establishes a strong correlation between the sub-nets accuracies and their converged accuracy. However, the key reason why the global BN can cause week correlations and why adaptive BN can establish a strong connection is never pointed out. It is not convincing to simply experimentally evaluate the baselines achieve lower correlations to support the claim.  
 
With this fatal deficiency, although the results seem empirical, it is hard to evaluate the methodical contribution of this work. Other questions are listed as follows. 
 
1). The right panel of Figure 5 is ambiguous. Is the horizontal axis represents the number of Iters? Can you illustrate the distance results more clearly?

content.title: Very constructive options
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive opinions. The authors appreciate your feedback as your concerns truly motivate us to largely revise the manuscript. To answer your questions:

Question1: it fails to state the motivation to adopt adaptive BN clearly.
Answer: we rephrased “Introduction” section, largely re-structured “Methodology” and “Experiments” sections to show a clearer presentation about our ideas. Especially, we newly added a “Motivation” as Section 3.1 to better clarify what motivates our idea. As a brief summary here, the main motivation of this work is the observation that the “vanilla evaluation” commonly used in existing works (Li et ak., 2016)(He et al., 2018c) provide a very low accuracy (in the scale of 0.01% to 0.1%) for the pruned candidates in our experiments, as pointed out by above comments from the area chair, but fine-tuning could boost it up to a normal range (scale of 10%). We doubt it that pruning candidates that ranks high in the evaluation of such low-range accuracy would also be likely to perform well after fine-tuning. This is called weak correlation provided by the vanilla evaluation in our work. We appreciate it if you may have a second time reading about our revised manuscript. 

Question 2: It fails to explain why global BN shows weak correlation while adaptive BN establishes strong correlation. 
Answer: This is a very important question. Thank you for pointing it out. We newly added Section 3.1 "Motivation" for a description with richer details. As a summary here, the global BN statistics are not adapted to the pruned network structures. So they mess up the inference accuracy during evaluation for the pruned networks. It also results in the low-range evaluation accuracy mentioend in the previous question. Adaptive BN re-calculates the BN statistocal values based on the pruned network connections, so it fixes this problem and brings the evaluation accuracy back to a normal range. Fine-tuning also does the same thing, but with a much higher computational cost (Table 2 in the revised manuscript).

Question 3: Figure 5 is ambiguous. 
Answer: we agree with this point, as also mentioned by many other readers. We have move this figure forwards as Figure 2 in our revised manuscript and added description in both the figure caption and textual description in the last paragraph in Section 3.1. As a summary here, each pixel is actually a distance of BN moving mean value from a channel and the heatmaps are 2D display of such distance values. The left sub-figure visualizes such distance between vanilla evaluation and the “true” mean values sampled from validation set. The right sub-figure shows the distance between values sampled from adaptive BN and the true mean values. The intuition is to show that adaptive BN provides statistics that are closer (bluer in the right sub-figure) to true statistics from the final testing phase on the validation set. That is the main reason our method provides much stronger correlation between the evaluated accuracy and the final inference accuracy on the validation dataset.

display_title: some confusion about the proposed method and some experiments setting

content.title: some confusion about the proposed method and some experiments setting
content.comment:
A neural network pruning method is proposed in this paper. The authors resort to Mentor Carlo sampling to approximate the Batch Normalization statistics, which is then used as an indicator for evaluating different pruning strategies. Some experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed FNNP. The experiment results are very impressive. 

I have some confusion about the proposed method and some experiments setting.
Major concern:
(1)The horizontal axis of Fig 4 is very strange. In terms of the BN-based method, all the accuracies are still very large (> 0.02), the accuracy is even larger than 0.3 for 75% FLOPs; while the accuracies of the PBN-based method are all less than 0.005. Giving that the accuracies of all methods are comparable after fine-tuning, the observation is quite strange.

(2) how to understand the right two sub-figures of Fig 5? What are the vertical axis and the horizontal axis? It seems there are some horizontal stripes, denoting a small deviation of the estimation, in the second figure. How to understand this observation?  

Some minor concerns:
(1) The full phrase of the abbreviation “BN” is missing.

(2) The proposed method requires the accessibility of a sufficient large validation dataset for reliable estimation, which is too strong for the real application. How the validation dataset is generated in this paper?

(3) It is claimed that "the proposed method does not change the parameter distribution". But it fails to elaborate in the main body.  Under the IID assumption, the PBM estimation also keeps the parameter distribution.

display_title: Reply to the area chair from the authors

content.title: Reply to the area chair from the authors
content.comment:
The authors appreciate your positive feedback to our work. You are definitely a responsible area chair. It is very unfortunate that our initial submitted manuscript did not reach a satisfying level of readability. So apart from rephrasing the textual expression, we re-organized the logic of presenting our idea. Apart from fixing all typos, we newly added "Motivation" section, restructured "Methodology" and "Experiments" section and largely rephrased "Introduction" section. We hope the improvement on the presentation could better deliver the essential thoughts behind.

Before answering the questions, an important change throughout the paper is that we change the naming for “using global Batch Normalization (BN) statistics in evaluation” from “PBN-based evaluation” to “vanilla evaluation”. This is clarified in the first paragraph in Section 3.1 (revised manuscript) and used throughout the paper.
  
Major concern (1) answer: It is also a surprise for us to observe such a large gap in accuracy between the our adaptive-BN evaluation and the vanilla evaluation. We added the explanation about this “low-range accuracy” to 1, 2, 5, 6 paragraphs in Section 3.1 in the revised manuscript. Vanilla evaluation uses “inappropriate” BN statistics to do inference and such globally sampled statistics are not adapted to the pruned connections of the sub-nets. This messes up the inference computation and leads to accuracy results in a very low range. Adaptive-BN, on the other side, fixes the statistics so that it shows accuracy in a way larger value range. Fine-tuning also fixes the BN statistics and show the same effects but it is time-consuming (Table 2). This is also illustrated by Figure 2 in the new manuscript, which is highly related to the below answer to your major concern (2) question.

Major concern (2) answer:  How to understand figure 5. This question points out an important information missing in our first manuscript and the authors apologize about it. This figure is now the Figure 2 in our new manuscript and explained with details in both the figure caption and in the last paragraph in Section 3.1. Each pixel is actually a distance of BN moving mean value from a channel and the heatmaps are 2D display of such distance values. The left sub-figure visualizes such distance between vanilla evaluation and the “true” mean values sampled from validation set. The right sub-figure shows the distance between values sampled from adaptive BN and the true mean values. The intuition is to show that adaptive BN provides statistics that are closer (bluer in the right sub-figure) to true statistics from the final testing phase on the validation set. That is the main reason our method provides much stronger correlation between the evaluated accuracy and the final inference accuracy on the validation dataset.

Minor concern (1) answer: Thank you for the careful reading! The first time this phrase appears in the paper is at the second page paragraph 1 in the new manuscript, where we added the full phrase. It is also added to the paragraph 2 in Section 3.1 as the abbreviation “BN” is used in a very high frequency since there.

Minor concern (2) answer: it is a very important detail that we failed to clarify in the initial manuscript. Thank you for pointing out.  Actually, we separately group 10000 data from the training dataset as the so called “validation set” in evaluation process, which is completely a different thing with the original validation dataset in the ImageNet dataset. To eliminate this confusion, we re-name this small group of data from training set as “sub-validation set”. This is pointed out in “Methodology” section (paragraph 3 page 6) and described in the experimental settings (paragraph 2 Section 4 in revised manuscript).

Minor concern (3) answer:  Our adaptive-BN-based method also keeps the parameter distribution. The intuition for this statement is to differentiate our method from (Ding et al., 2019), (Wen et al., 2016), (Liu et al., 2017), (Yu et al., 2018), (Zhuang et al., 2018), and (Gordon et al., 2018) etc., which change the parameter distribution as part of their strategy for better pruning (paragraph 2 Section 2). This point is not a strong argument for any claimed advantages, so we removed it in the new manuscript.

As you comment, this work gives us really good results. It achieves the state-of-the-art pruning performance by outperforming all of our studied methods in this domain. Our github repository also gained 35 stars at this early stage without any advertisement from the authors. The new version is very different with the first upload. If it’s not a huge bothering, we sincerely invite you to have a re-reading about our revised version of manuscript. Thank you.
